location: No breaking step. All steps were checked: the P2 decomposition, the first-term bound via P3, the second and third terms via P4, the combination with P6 for (ii), and the choice of constants.
objection: I found no error. The proof only puts the dependencies together, and each one is used inside its stated hypotheses. (1) P2 holds for real x≥1 and q∈ℕ. Its MT, Q, D_x and V are the same objects as in the statement: the MT formula and the definitions of A_0, η and m_t(q) match word for word. (2) In the sum over 1≤h≤x/q, each m=hq is an integer with 1≤m≤x, and x≥2. That is exactly the range of P3, which gives the uniform bound c_3(ε)x^{2/3+ε}. There are ⌊x/q⌋≤x/q terms, so the sum is at most 2c_3 x^{5/3+ε}/q. The term count and the summed bound are both right. (3) P4(i) and P4(ii) are used with x≥1 and 1≤q≤x, as P4 requires. The step 2x·c_0√x/q = 2c_0x^{3/2}/q ≤ 2c_0x^{5/3+ε}/q holds because x≥1. (4) Take c_7=2c_3+2c_0. It bounds the coefficient of x^{5/3+ε}/q and also the coefficient c_0 of √x, since c_3≥0. It depends only on ε, because c_0 is absolute. (5) P6 is used for x≥1 and 1≤q≤x, and its h(q) matches the statement exactly. Taking c=max(c_6,c_7) gives both (i) and (ii) with the ranges and error terms as stated, uniformly in q. The proof interchanges no limits and cites no external literature, so no post-2010 source is used.
other_issues: Cosmetic only: the proof says it needs x≥2 for P3. That is correct, but it is the only reason the statement has x≥2 rather than x≥1. The proof could say this explicitly; it is not an error.
